I heard Google is working on it. This is a side effect, from what I understand, the sandboxing of tabs and processes.

Yes, basically Chrome spawns separate processes for each tab, for security reasons. This was hailed as a great innovation and game-changer for the web when Chrome was launched 6 years ago. (I still remember reading the comic that accompanied the launch and being fascinated with the sandboxing and new JS engine.)

I think part of the backlash is due to the shift in focus from power to efficiency. In the past decade we stopped making things faster and started making them use less energy, less space. So we have laptops, netbooks with lower raw specs but much higher efficiency. With these constrained devices, Chrome’s memory usage suddenly looked a lot higher in proportion. So you have all these people worrying about Chrome using 1GB RAM when they only have 2GB.

On my machine with 16GB RAM though, I don’t even care…

i don't hear you bitch and moan about today's websites and their needlessly heavily euntime-optimized javascript and other client-side scripting, with DOM and graphics and animations and all that jazz.

the 'browser' today has become an operating system on its own with an entire GUI shoved in it for good measure. Provides its own runtime environment, does system abstraction and program ("website") isolation. Deal with it.

Calling a browser an "operating system" is a touch hyperbolic. It is, first and last, a GUI. Everything else, network access, disk access, lights and sound all go through the actual OS. System abstraction? That is a user space concern, where there are endless layers of system abstraction, allowing a monkey in India to write a Single Page Application to check stock prices.
chrome os, firefox os... do you understand where i'm getting at?

Those aren't a browser alone though, they still depend on the services of the Linux kernel and related subsystems to provide networking, graphics, hardware abstraction, as well as APIs and libraries to allow the operation of the sole userland program that runs under each system.

FYI, Firefox OS is also extended by using Android's services and platforms in addition to Linux, making your point even more so moot.

my point is "more moot" (which is something syntacticaly correct but absurd) because firefox os can be even more bloated?

my point, is that browsers now have become very bloated and complicated, mostly due to the demands of modern popular webpages. You don't like chrome or firefox eating all that much memory, go ahead and use lynx/linksor another bare minimum browser.

I do have to agree that the current major browsers are inefficient, but mostly due not to the demands, but the badly implemented resource allocation by the engine. At least from Webkit alone, one could make a low memory, highly compatible browser without having to hand out for extreme sandboxing and process separation. Just look at Mobile Safari on iOS or the hundreds of system apps on OS X that use Webkit in one way or another.

A few projects have risen in the wake of these issues (namely Pale Moon, Midori and TenFourFox) which I applaud for filling the niche of low-memory, low CPU power devices. It is now left for the major players to change their directions (and hopefully the open source community helps it get there).

Has anyone played this game? How is it?

I played it for about a month or two at launch (stopped due to being unable to pay for sub at the time) and recently resubbed. It is a very good MMO, and honestly I'm surprised it's currently not doing very well. The combat system and dungeons are top-notch, I'm a big fan of the art style, and the humor/story is well done and not over-the-top like in WoW. I think it's one of the best MMOs out there, but the subscription model is out-dated at this point and drove people away.
So the numbers should come back when it goes free-to-play. I might try it out then, thanks!

At launch there were tons of bugs. There were a lot of problems that should have been addressed before release and they just spent the next year fixing them. Couple that with seldom content patches, a lack of content outside hardcore raids for endgame, unbalanced PVP, huge attunement grind for raids, No 'easy mode' dungeons and people started leaving in droves to the point where now there are only 2 servers and one of them is essentially dead.

I played it for a couple weeks when it first came out but eventually got a refund. Not because it wasn't fun, but it was competing with my WoW time and I couldn't do both. Now that I don't play WoW anymore, I might return to the game.

It was satisfying clearing each zone as you leveled up. I don't know what end game was like though.

I moved to Wildstar after the Honorbuddy ban wave about a month ago.

World of Warcraft has got progressively worse every expansion to the point I could no longer bring myself to play it and started botting.

By comparison, Wildstar is amazing, the combat is brilliantly done, it's quite hard, if you fuck up, you die (no loss of items).

The humour and cartoonish artwork is done really well and the coarse language is not over the top, one time my Warrior leveled and the narrator/voice over said "OOhhh FUUUCK Yeah!", and a welcome change from the overly PC WoW (I once received a 48 hour ban for rolling an Orc Death Knight named "Führer").

Wildstar is definitely worth trying.

I’m excited to try it. The visuals are obviously attractive to a former WoW addict, and I’ve heard good things about the combat, like the telegraphing of attacks. It just launched at the wrong time when people were no longer interested in paying for a subscription MMO.
